source.title: Causal Scrubbing: a method for rigorously testing interpretability hypotheses [Redwood Research]
source.authors: LawrenceC; Adrià Garriga-alonso; Nicholas Goldowsky-Dill; ryan_greenblatt; jenny; Ansh Radhakrishnan; Buck; Nate Thomas

record.tranche_reason: Uses causal scrubbing, a resampling-ablation method, to test a mechanistic hypothesis about induction in a two-layer attention-only model; this is a different method from the original study's evidence.
record.gate_note: The induction results in section 5.2 are relevant to V1. The parentheses-checker results are about a different task. Results cited from other work and commenters' later reports are not rows.
record.test_reason: Causal scrubbing (resampling ablations) tests whether the V1 circuit explains induction-head behaviour in a 2-layer attention-only model. This is a different method aimed at V1's mechanism. The post is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report 35% recovery for the naive induction hypothesis and 86% after adding pathways. They conclude that causal scrubbing let them build and trust a more precise hypothesis than ad-hoc methods would. They describe hypotheses as reasonably but not completely accurate.
record.recipe_differences: Uses causal scrubbing via resampling ablations to test a detailed mechanistic hypothesis, rather than the original study's methods for identifying and measuring induction heads and their training dynamics.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported recovery changes with hypothesis specificity and included pathways: 35% for the naive hypothesis and 86% for the refined hypothesis. The evaluation uses a subset selected for cases where induction is likely, but not guaranteed, to help.
record.problems: The induction evidence summarized here concerns one 2-layer attention-only model. The evaluation subset is selected because induction is likely, but not guaranteed, to help, and the actual next token may not be the token induction predicts. The post gives no uncertainty estimates for these recovery figures and points to an auxiliary post for detailed results.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant results are reported in this post. The parentheses-checker results in section 5.1 concern a different behavior and are omitted.

untested.parts: Only one 2-layer attention-only model on a filtered OpenWebText subset. No synthetic repeated-sequence [A][B]…[A] test. No check across several small models.

record.verdict_notes: Buck's later comment argues the results show induction heads are not the simple circuit people claimed. He quotes figures like 20% and says he is unsure how to interpret them. This is post-hoc commentary and not a row. Detailed induction results are in the auxiliary post (part 4 of 5), which is not included here.

versions.untested_parts: Tests mechanistic hypotheses on one 2-layer attention-only model and an induction-focused subset; does not establish the mechanism across multiple small transformers or directly test every instance of the [A][B] … [A] → [B] pattern.
No training-time trajectory, formation window, in-context-learning gain over token position, or training-loss bump is measured.
No test of whether induction heads explain most in-context learning in large transformers.
No comparison across model families, sizes, training runs, architectures, or modalities.
Uses an induction-focused OpenWebText subset, but does not vary data or training setup to test effects on formation or persistence.
Does not compare few-shot task learning with copying or test whether other mechanisms carry most few-shot learning.
Does not measure formation over training or test whether it consists of multiple transitions.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only model
rows.operation_detail: Causal scrubbing with resampling ablations of activations, testing a naive induction hypothesis that assigns values and queries to token embeddings and keys to the previous-token output of layer 0.

conditions.value: subset of OpenWebText where induction is likely, but not guaranteed, to be helpful

rows.note: The post says this hypothesis only recovers 35% of performance on the selected dataset.
rows.check: Row is correct. This naive hypothesis is the direct encoding of V1: keys come from previous-token attention in layer 0, queries and values from embeddings. The baseline normalization for the induction metric is not given in this post; footnote 16's normalization covers only the paren task.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only model
rows.operation_detail: Causal scrubbing with a refined hypothesis allowing three-token comparisons, current-position layer-0 contributions to queries and values, and three specified layer-0 heads that attend to repeated occurrences of the current token.

conditions.value: subset of OpenWebText where induction is likely, but not guaranteed, to be helpful
refined induction hypothesis with additional pathways

rows.note: The post reports that the refined hypothesis recovers 86% of performance; the hypothesis allows more pathways than the naive version.
rows.check: Row is correct, but the refined hypothesis goes beyond V1. It needs 3-token comparison, current-position layer-0 input to queries and values, and three layer-0 duplicate-token heads. It is evidence that V1 must be extended, not a straight confirmation.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, refinements and paragraph reporting 86%; footnotes 19–20.

relationships.condition: Naive previous-token-head → induction-head hypothesis, 2-layer attn-only model, induction-favouring OpenWebText subset
relationships.reason: The pure V1 circuit recovers only 35% of performance, so the simple composition account leaves most of the behaviour unexplained (r1).
relationships.display_finding: The simple previous-token-to-induction circuit recovered only 35% of performance.
